results.assessment: The brief has real force on the lockout facts: it clearly presents a self-help exclusion from the residence and a colorable argument that Chapter 1923 process was required before Alice was barred. Its biggest weakness is that it never cleanly establishes the landlord-tenant predicate for R.C. 5321.15 and Chapter 1923, relying instead on occupancy language that can read like a permissive guest arrangement. It is also vulnerable on summary judgment because it does not plainly show specific evidence tying those facts to each essential element. The nominal-damages point is not a separate rescue if conversion itself is not established. The research leaves the tenant-status gap unresolved.

results.assessment: The brief has a usable overall structure and its summary-judgment framing is serviceable, but as written it is exposed on the points that matter most. The biggest problems are that it does not clearly establish a protected possessory status for Chapter 1923 and it does not show competent summary-judgment evidence of conversion for specific property. The Civ.R. 56 discussion also needs tightening so it does not overstate the movants’ burden. The conclusion is thin because it simply depends on those disputed premises rather than adding an independent basis for reversal. The research leaves the core standard and the main vulnerabilities settled, not open.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real liability problem on this record. The cited Ohio material, as summarized in the record, supports the defense point that negligence per se depends on a statute or ordinance that protects the plaintiff's class and the type of injury, and that the absence of privity is not enough by itself. The brief invokes CCO 240.04(e), R.C. 3742.37, and R.C. 5321.04, but it never squarely shows that those provisions create a private damages remedy for later occupants after transfer. The brief gestures to 'intended beneficiary' and to lead-hazard policy, but that is not the same thing as a statute-backed duty running to these plaintiffs.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not ask this Court to invent a free-standing private right of action under the City Code or Chapter 3742. Rather, they rely on the mandatory duties imposed by CCO 240.04(e), R.C. 3742.37, and R.C. 5321.04 as the source of the duty element in negligence per se, with proximate cause and damages supplied by ordinary Ohio tort principles. The ordinances and statutes were enacted to prevent childhood lead exposure, and Stark’s admitted failure to comply with the abatement order may therefore be pleaded as a statutory breach that supports civil liability when that breach proximately results in the very harm the provisions were designed to prevent.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Recast the negligence-per-se point as a duty-and-breach theory, not as an argument that the ordinances themselves create an express private damages action for later occupants. The brief needs to say that it relies on the mandatory abatement duties as the standard of conduct, while Ohio tort law supplies the damages remedy.

challenges.opponent_argument: Ohio law does not support the brief's attempt to keep a former owner's obligations alive after transfer of the property. The source summarized in the record states that, absent an agreement or law to the contrary, prior owners are divested of all rights and obligations when title transfers. That is the opposite of the rule Appellants need here. Their reliance on Restatement § 840A asks the Court to create a new post-transfer liability rule, not apply existing Ohio law.
challenges.why_it_matters: If obligations ended when Stark transferred the property, the post-transfer nuisance theory fails.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands well. The record source summarized in the brief itself points the other way: prior owners are divested of rights and obligations on transfer absent an agreement or law to the contrary. That directly undercuts the attempt to keep Stark on the hook after foreclosure or sale. The brief's answer is mostly to cite Restatement sections and out-of-state nuisance cases; it does not identify Ohio authority adopting a continuing post-transfer duty in this setting. If the court accepts the Ohio divestiture rule, the post-transfer nuisance theory fails.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not contend that a mere transfer of title magically creates a new duty. They contend that Stark’s liability arose from its own conduct while it owned the property: Stark received actual notice of the lead hazard, was ordered to abate it, was given time to comply, and failed to do so before relinquishing the premises. The later transfer did not undo that completed breach or erase the consequences of Stark’s earlier failure to correct a known nuisance condition.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop arguing that Ohio already recognizes a broad post-transfer liability rule unless you can supply Ohio authority for that proposition. Reframe the point around Stark’s own pre-transfer failure to obey the order and abate the hazard, which the complaint alleges occurred while Stark still owned the property.

challenges.opponent_argument: The common-law negligence theory still fails for lack of a duty owed to these later occupants. The brief cites only general negligence principles, but the Ohio authority summarized in the record recognizes that former owners are divested of obligations upon transfer absent contrary law. That leaves no pleaded common-law duty from Stark to the Carters after Stark relinquished the property, so the negligence count cannot proceed.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a duty, there is no common-law negligence claim to reverse back into the case.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a strong companion attack to a3 and reaches the common-law negligence theory directly. The brief tries to supply duty with general reasonable-care language and foreseeability, but the record authority the defense can invoke says former owners are ordinarily out of the picture once title passes unless some contrary law keeps obligations alive. The brief does not supply a concrete Ohio common-law duty owed by a former owner to later tenants after transfer. If the court buys this, the common-law negligence claim goes out even if negligence per se is rejected.
challenges.suggested_response: Even apart from the statutory and ordinance-based duties, Appellants alleged a common-law duty arising from Stark’s ownership and actual notice of a known dangerous condition. Stark allegedly knew the premises contained lead hazards, had the ability and opportunity to correct them, and chose not to do so before relinquishing the property. That is sufficient at the pleading stage to allege breach of a duty owed while Stark still controlled the premises; the subsequent transfer does not eliminate the alleged negligent omission that occurred beforehand.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue a free-standing common-law duty from a former owner to later occupants unless the brief can support it with authority not in the current record. Recast the duty point as Stark’s duty while it was owner and had actual notice, and say the complaint alleges that Stark breached that duty before transfer.

challenges.opponent_argument: The causation allegations are too speculative to survive dismissal. The record authority states that proximate causation must be established, and damages cannot rest on conjecture or speculation. Here, the brief leaps from a 2005 abatement order and later transfer/foreclosure to a later child's injury without pleading facts showing when the child was actually exposed, who controlled the premises at that time, or why Stark's conduct rather than later ownership or conditions caused the harm.
challenges.why_it_matters: If causation is speculative, the claims fail even if some duty could be shown.

The source summarized in the record states that, absent an agreement or law to the contrary, prior owners are divested of all rights and obligations when title transfers. That is the opposite of the rule Appellants need here. Their reliance on Restatement § 840A asks the Court to create a new post-transfer liability rule, not apply existing Ohio law.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a real liability problem on this record. The cited Ohio material, as summarized in the record, supports the defense point that negligence per se depends on a statute or ordinance that protects the plaintiff's class and the type of injury, and that the absence of privity is not enough by itself. The brief invokes CCO 240.04(e), R.C. 3742.37, and R.C. 5321.04, but it never squarely shows that those provisions create a private damages remedy for later occupants after transfer. The brief gestures to 'intended beneficiary' and to lead-hazard policy, but that is not the same thing as a statute-backed duty running to these plaintiffs.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It argues that CCO 240.04(e), R.C. 5321.04, and R.C. 3742.38 support negligence per se, that the City ordered Stark to abate the hazard, and that the Carters were intended beneficiaries rather than incidental ones.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Ohio appellate or Supreme Court authority treats lead-hazard abatement provisions as creating a private damages claim for later occupants, and whether the protected-class / injury-type requirement is satisfied here.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands well. The record source summarized in the brief itself points the other way: prior owners are divested of rights and obligations on transfer absent an agreement or law to the contrary. That directly undercuts the attempt to keep Stark on the hook after foreclosure or sale. The brief's answer is mostly to cite Restatement sections and out-of-state nuisance cases; it does not identify Ohio authority adopting a continuing post-transfer duty in this setting. If the court accepts the Ohio divestiture rule, the post-transfer nuisance theory fails.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It relies on Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 840A and 373, DiCenzo, Olpp, Minaya, and Kurtigian to argue that a vendor who created or maintained a nuisance can remain liable after transfer.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether any Ohio case has adopted Restatement §§ 840A or 373 for lead-hazard or nuisance claims after transfer, and whether foreclosure changes the divestiture analysis.

results.verdict: persuasive in framing but vulnerable on duty and causation
results.assessment: The brief reads coherently and its strongest feature is the effort to tie Stark’s own pre-transfer failure to abate a known hazard to the later injury. But it is exposed on the central legal theory: it never clearly shows that the cited ordinances and statutes create a private damages duty for later occupants, and the transfer-of-title point is a serious obstacle to any post-transfer liability theory. The common-law negligence count is also thin on a concrete duty owed after transfer, and the causation allegations are vulnerable as too inferential. The procedural conversion point has some force, but it is less decisive than the duty defects.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable pleading-stage narrative: it repeatedly alleges notice, a mandatory abatement order, failure to remediate, and continuing injury, which helps on causation and plausibility. But its biggest weakness is the central legal theory that liability survives transfer of title; the cited Ohio authority cuts against that, and the brief does not supply controlling Ohio law to bridge the gap. The negligence-per-se section is also underdeveloped because the cited duties do not clearly extend to a former owner after title passes. The Restatement argument is only persuasive in the abstract, not enough to cure the authority problem.

challenges.opponent_argument: The requested sanction is overbroad. The brief identifies alleged failures to order a transcript, serve filings, and conform the brief to App.R. 16, but it does not show that those defects automatically require dismissal and striking the entire appeal rather than simply limiting review to the existing record or disregarding defective material. The brief asks for the harshest possible remedy without supplying authority tying these alleged rule violations to mandatory dismissal.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court rejects the sanction request, the appeal remains alive and the court must reach the merits instead of ending the case on procedure alone.

target.excerpt: I.  APPELLANT'S APPEAL SHOULD BE DISMISSED FOR FAILING TO COMPLY WITH RULES OF APPELLATE PROCEDURE AND THE COURT'S ORDER.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real attack on the remedy, but it does not fully defeat the appellees on this record. Ohio authority generally treats failure to file a transcript or comply with briefing rules as grounds to limit review or sanction the appellant, not as an automatic dismissal in every case. That said, the brief adds a stronger fact: the court entered a specific order to complete the record by June 18, 2007 and appellant admittedly did not comply. On that record, dismissal is at least available as a discretionary sanction, so the attack only lands on the point that the brief overstates the remedy as if it were mandatory. The request to strike the whole brief is the weaker part; the record-rule and transcript objections do not by themselves require that sanction.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s repeated failures to comply with the Appellate Rules and this Court’s May 30, 2007 order requiring completion of the record by June 18, 2007 warrant dismissal of this appeal in this Court’s discretion. Appellant did not provide a transcript, did not complete the record as ordered, and has relied on materials outside the record. At a minimum, if the Court declines to dismiss the appeal, its review should be confined to the record transmitted from the trial court and should not include any extra-record materials or unsupported factual assertions.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the request. Do not present dismissal and striking the brief as mandatory; instead argue that dismissal is warranted in the Court’s discretion because Appellant failed to comply with App.R. 9(B), App.R. 13(B), App.R. 16, and this Court’s May 30, 2007 order requiring completion of the record by June 18, 2007. Add an alternative request that, if the Court does not dismiss, it should confine review to the existing record and disregard any extra-record material.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even accepting the premise that some attachments are outside the appellate record, the proper response is to ignore those materials, not to strike the whole appeal or treat every factual assertion as unusable. The brief itself distinguishes between extra-record exhibits and the merits of the underlying eviction; that distinction cuts against the sweeping request to exclude everything Appellant filed.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court narrows the remedy to disregarding only truly extra-record matter, Appellant can still obtain review of any preserved, record-based issues.

target.excerpt: MATTERS CONTAINED IN APPELLANT'S BRIEF OUTSIDE OF THE RECORD SHOULD BE STRICKEN.

challenges.coaching_recommendation: Replace the sweeping request to strike the entire appeal with a narrower request to disregard only the exhibits, photographs, and factual assertions that were never made part of the trial court record.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest in insisting that the appeal be decided only on the record and that extra-record exhibits and factual assertions be disregarded. It is weaker where it asks for the harshest remedy: dismissal and striking the whole appeal are framed too absolutely, and the brief needs to explain why the specific rule violations justify that remedy rather than simply limiting review. The repair-defense argument also overreaches by treating the absence of an escrow deposit as if it automatically wipes out all repair-related evidence; it is safer as a defense to this nonpayment record than as a categorical statement about all landlord-repair remedies.

queries: Ohio appellate brief deficient no citations to authority no record citations App.R. 16 substantial compliance dismissal disfavored affirm on merits

challenges.judge_assessment: Authority cuts against automatic dismissal. The cited source points to appellate-brief deficiencies generally being handled through substantial-compliance/merits review rather than jurisdictional dismissal, so appellee's request to strike the brief and dismiss the appeal is vulnerable if the court wants to reach the merits. The brief does identify App.R. 9(B), 13(B), and 16 problems and the missed record order, but it does not cite authority showing those defects require the extreme sanction it seeks. Appellee stands to lose the dismissal/strike remedy; the court may instead deny that request and decide the appeal on the existing record or under the presumption of regularity.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant's failure to provide a transcript and to comply with this Court's May 30, 2007 order leaves the record incomplete. As a result, any factual assertions that depend on materials outside the record cannot be considered. The proper course is not dismissal, but affirmance of the trial court's October 6, 2006 Decision and Order on the record as filed.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Withdraw the request to dismiss the appeal or strike the brief. Keep the point that Appellant failed to provide a transcript, failed to comply with the Court's May 30, 2007 order, and relied on material outside the record, but ask the Court to disregard any unsupported material and affirm on the record before it.

challenges.opponent_argument: The escrow argument is too broad. Chapter 5321 does recognize landlord duties and tenant remedies for noncompliance, including rent abatement and damages, and Ohio authority recognizes that repair and habitability issues can matter in eviction litigation. The brief therefore cannot convert the absence of an escrow deposit into a categorical rule that no repair-related defense exists at all.
challenges.why_it_matters: If escrow is not an absolute prerequisite to every repair-related defense, the trial court's rejection of the defense cannot be affirmed on the broad rule the brief states.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real but limited attack. The broader landlord-tenant statutes do recognize tenant remedies and some authority treats repair/habitability issues as potentially relevant in eviction litigation, so appellee overstates matters when it frames the escrow omission as a categorical bar to any repair-based defense. But on this record the brief already cites Smith and Martins Ferry for the escrow prerequisite, and it relies on the admitted nonpayment of May and June rent plus the admitted failure to escrow rent. That makes the defense weak here even if the appellee's statement of the rule is broader than necessary. Appellee mainly risks overclaiming the breadth of the rule, not the bottom-line affirmance.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if Ohio law recognizes tenant remedies for landlord noncompliance in appropriate cases, those remedies do not assist Appellant here. Appellant admitted that he and his wife failed to pay rent for May and June 2006, and he admitted that neither he nor his wife deposited rent in escrow under R.C. 5321.07. Under Smith v. Wright and Martins Ferry Jaycee Housing, Inc. v. Pawlaczyk, the condition of the premises does not supply a valid defense to restitution where the tenant is not current in rent and has not used the statutory escrow remedy. The trial court therefore correctly rejected the repair-based defense and granted restitution.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Qualify the escrow rule. Do not suggest that repair issues can never matter in an eviction case; instead argue that, on these facts, the repair defense fails because Appellant admitted the rent default and admitted no escrow deposit under R.C. 5321.07.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even taking the brief's theory at face value, its own authorities cut against a holdover-tenant defense. The Ohio materials supplied here describe R.C. 5321.03 as barring retaliation defenses when the statutory exceptions apply, and they note that Indian Hills and Samsa were applied to tenants who became holdover tenants after the lease expired. Ms. Masten's own timeline in the brief shows a fixed-term lease, a nonrenewal notice, expiration of the term, and only then a forcible-entry-and-detainer action. That is the holdover posture the Ohio authorities treat as dispositive.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest counter. The cited Ohio materials do support the premise that Chapter 5321’s retaliation defense has a holdover exception, and the brief’s own facts show a fixed-term lease, nonrenewal, expiration, and only then eviction. The brief tries to answer by distinguishing Chapter 4112 and by invoking FHA preemption, but on this record the court can still read Indian Hills/Samsa as controlling the holdover-possession point in the state-law posture. If the panel accepts that framing, Ms. Masten loses the holdover-based retaliation defense on Count One.
challenges.suggested_response: Indian Hills and the later holdover cases addressed the Ohio landlord-tenant retaliation statute and the statutory possession rules, not a federal Fair Housing Act claim. Ms. Masten does not ask this Court to create a right to remain after lease expiration; she asks only that the Court not extend a state holdover-possession rule to defeat a claim that the nonrenewal itself was taken because she aided and encouraged protected fair-housing activity and filed her own charge. Under 42 U.S.C. 3617, it is unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with a person because she exercised or aided another in exercising fair-housing rights, and nothing in Indian Hills supplies authority for extinguishing that federal protection merely because the landlord waited until the lease term expired before filing for possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow this point to say Indian Hills and Samsa resolve only the Ohio landlord-tenant retaliation issue in the holdover-possession setting, not a federal Fair Housing Act claim under 42 U.S.C. 3617. The brief should not overstate that Chapter 4112 itself supplies a holdover defense; instead, it should argue that the trial court could not use the state holdover rule to bar a distinct federal retaliation claim.

challenges.judge_assessment: The preemption point is directionally sound but not airtight. Section 3615 is about state laws that require or permit discriminatory housing practices, and the brief does not show that Indian Hills or the Ohio possession statutes literally command discrimination. On the other hand, the brief’s theory is that applying those state rules to bar an FHA retaliation defense conflicts with federal rights, and it cites general preemption cases for that proposition. The court could accept or reject that framing. If the attack wins, Ms. Masten loses the Supremacy Clause route, but not necessarily the underlying FHA argument.
challenges.suggested_response: This is an as-applied conflict, not a facial attack on Ohio landlord-tenant law. Section 3615 provides that any state law that purports to require or permit a discriminatory housing practice is invalid to that extent, and the Supremacy Clause requires state law to give way where it conflicts with federal law. Accordingly, if Indian Hills and the holdover rule are applied here to bar a defense that the nonrenewal was taken because Ms. Masten aided and exercised fair-housing rights, they must yield to the federal protection afforded by 42 U.S.C. 3617.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the preemption section to an as-applied conflict argument. Say the brief is not attacking Ohio law wholesale; it is arguing only that, to the extent Indian Hills and the holdover rule would bar a federal fair-housing retaliation defense, they are preempted under 42 U.S.C. 3615 and the Supremacy Clause.

results.verdict: partly persuasive but exposed on the holdover and causation
results.assessment: The brief has a coherent fairness narrative and its best point is that it tries to frame the dispute as a federal fair-housing retaliation claim rather than a routine possession case. But as written it is vulnerable in three places: it leans too hard on Chapter 4112 silence to create a possession defense, its Supremacy Clause theory is broader than the authorities it cites, and its proof of retaliation depends heavily on chronology and an OCRC probable-cause finding without enough support that those facts alone establish motive. The holdover posture in the record remains the hardest obstacle, and the research does not settle that Chapter 4112 or the FHA displaces the state possession framework on these facts.

challenges.opponent_argument: Section 3617 does not prove itself. The supplied Ohio retaliation materials say the defense must be established by evidence and discuss the dual-motive problem; they do not say timing alone is enough. Here, the brief relies primarily on sequence—protected activity, then nonrenewal, then eviction—and an OCRC probable-cause finding, but that does not, by itself, establish that the nonrenewal was because of protected activity rather than because the lease expired and Ms. Masten stayed beyond term.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without competent proof of causation, the FHA retaliation theory does not defeat summary judgment.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is supported by the cited retaliation materials and it hits the weakest part of the federal FHA theory: causation. The brief does more than timing alone—it cites Matarese, the OCRC probable-cause finding, and the sequence of events—but it still does not produce direct evidence tying K&D's nonrenewal decision to protected activity. On this record, a court could conclude the retaliation theory is too inferential to defeat summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: Retaliation is rarely proved by direct evidence, and circumstantial evidence is sufficient. Here, Ms. Masten showed that she assisted another tenant in filing a discrimination charge, filed her own charge, K&D knew of that protected activity, and the nonrenewal followed shortly thereafter. The Ohio Civil Rights Commission’s probable-cause determination further supports an inference that the stated reason for the nonrenewal was pretextual. On this record, a reasonable trier of fact could find the nonrenewal causally connected to Ms. Masten’s protected activity, and summary judgment was therefore improper.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that the retaliation case is circumstantial, then press that circumstantial proof is enough to create a factual dispute. Recast the OCRC finding and the timing as part of a broader causation showing, not as timing alone.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Chapter 4112 distinction is not enough. The brief assumes that because Chapter 4112 does not repeat the landlord-tenant holdover language, Indian Hills cannot apply. But the supplied Ohio materials still recognize the holdover framework in eviction law, and the fair-housing materials do not create a rule that a tenant who remains after lease expiration may always defeat possession simply by alleging retaliation. The absence of identical wording does not supply the missing right.
challenges.why_it_matters: The Ohio Fair Housing Act theory still fails if the holdover framework remains applicable to possession actions.

challenges.judge_assessment: The cited Ohio materials support the landlord's side more than the brief does: the holdover exception is a real feature of Ohio retaliation law, and source 24 expressly discusses it. The brief's answer is the statutory-text distinction between Chapter 4112 and Chapter 5321, but that step is underdeveloped. A court could accept the cross-application of Indian Hills and hold that the absence of identical wording in Chapter 4112 does not create a separate holdover escape from possession.
challenges.suggested_response: Ohio courts commonly look to federal precedent for guidance in construing the Ohio Fair Housing Act. Wooten v. Columbus, Div. of Water, 91 Ohio App.3d 326; Matthews v. New Century Mortg. Corp., 185 F. Supp.2d 874. For that reason, Indian Hills should not be extended to foreclose a Chapter 4112 fair-housing retaliation defense where the alleged nonrenewal followed protected activity. Indian Hills addressed the landlord-tenant retaliation statute; it did not hold that a holdover tenant is categorically barred from asserting fair-housing rights under Chapter 4112.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Reframe the Chapter 4112 point as one of statutory construction and limitation, not as proof that the absence of identical holdover language creates a new defense. If the brief wants an independent Ohio Fair Housing Act holding, it needs direct Chapter 4112 authority that is not in the current record.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Supremacy Clause argument overstates the conflict. The supplied authority on Ohio eviction law treats federal and Ohio fair-housing statutes as parallel sources of defense when discrimination is actually shown; it does not say the Fair Housing Act displaces ordinary state possession rules whenever a tenant invokes retaliation. Nothing in the authorities cited here shows that 42 U.S.C. § 3615 invalidates the Ohio holdover rule or Indian Hills' possession analysis.
challenges.why_it_matters: If there is no actual conflict, the state court was not required to discard Ohio eviction precedent.

challenges.judge_assessment: The Supremacy Clause point is legally real, but the attack is strong because the brief never cleanly identifies an actual conflict between Indian Hills/Ohio possession law and the federal Fair Housing Act. The cited authorities support preemption only when state law actually conflicts with federal law; they do not themselves show that Ohio's holdover rule is preempted. The brief does cite §3615 and preemption cases, so this is answerable, but if the court sees no direct conflict, the Supremacy Clause theory fails.
challenges.suggested_response: To the extent the trial court applied Indian Hills and R.C. 5321.03 to bar a defense based on federally protected fair-housing activity, that application conflicts with 42 U.S.C. § 3617 and must yield under 42 U.S.C. § 3615. Ohio courts may look to state possession rules in ordinary eviction cases, but they may not apply those rules in a way that nullifies a federal right Congress has made enforceable. At minimum, the Ohio authorities should be construed consistently with the federal Fair Housing Act rather than used to extinguish it.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that the Supremacy Clause automatically erases the Ohio possession rule. Instead, say the trial court’s application of Indian Hills conflicts with the federal right only to the extent it bars a defense based on protected fair-housing activity, and ask the court to construe the Ohio rule consistently with federal law.

challenges.opponent_argument: The holdover-status point is still dispositive under the Ohio materials supplied here. The managed content states that R.C. 5321.03 bars a retaliation defense when one of its statutory exceptions applies, and the same Ohio eviction materials explain the holdover exception in the possession context. Once the lease expired and Ms. Masten remained, K&D had the statutory path to possession that Indian Hills recognized; relabeling the dispute as a Fair Housing Act retaliation claim does not erase the holdover posture or the statutory limit on the defense.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the holdover exception applies, Count One was properly resolved on summary judgment regardless of the retaliation label.

challenges.judge_assessment: The Ohio authorities do support the proposition that holdover status matters in the Chapter 5321 retaliation context, but that does not by itself defeat the federal FHA framing of this unit. The brief already answers by shifting away from Ohio landlord-tenant law and arguing that federal fair-housing rights survive the holdover label. So this attack has force only against the state-law strand, not the federal one.
challenges.suggested_response: Indian Hills should not be applied to foreclose Ms. Masten’s federal fair-housing defense merely because she remained in possession after the lease term expired. The issue is not whether K&D served the notices required for a forcible-entry-and-detainer action; it is whether the nonrenewal and eviction were taken because Ms. Masten aided another tenant and exercised her own rights under the Fair Housing Act. Where the challenged conduct is protected by 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604 and 3617, the holdover label does not extinguish the federal defense.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the holdover argument, but narrow it: do not rely on the existence of a general retaliation defense alone. Tie the point to the federal Fair Housing Act and say Indian Hills should not be read to bar a federally protected defense to possession when the eviction is alleged to have followed protected fair-housing activity.

challenges.opponent_argument: The public-policy attack cannot do the work the brief assigns it. The supplied materials show that retaliation defenses and holdover possession are governed by statute and established eviction doctrine; they do not provide authority for overriding Indian Hills on a generalized fairness theory. Put differently, policy concerns do not supply the missing statutory elements or erase the holdover exception the Ohio materials discuss.
challenges.why_it_matters: If policy cannot override the statutory framework, the request to reverse Indian Hills on policy grounds fails.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is not a complete answer to the brief's last assignment. The cited materials and the brief's own argument show a policy concern, but they do not establish that an intermediate Ohio appellate court can overrule Indian Hills on policy alone. The brief already tries to ground the policy point in retaliation statutes and analogous public-policy cases, so the attack lands only as a warning that policy rhetoric is not a substitute for a doctrinal basis.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if Indian Hills remains good law on its facts, it should not be extended to immunize retaliatory nonrenewal of a lease. A rule that bars tenants from raising retaliation after a lease expires chills the reporting of housing discrimination and discourages tenants from assisting other residents in the exercise of their fair-housing rights. At minimum, Indian Hills should be limited to the Chapter 5321 retaliation context and should not be read as a blanket bar to fair-housing defenses.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tone down the request to reverse Indian Hills on public policy alone. Use policy as a reason not to extend the case beyond Chapter 5321, and keep the doctrinal anchor on the Fair Housing Act and Ohio courts’ use of federal precedent.

attacks_proposed.argument: The holdover-status point is still dispositive under the Ohio materials supplied here. The managed content states that R.C. 5321.03 bars a retaliation defense when one of its statutory exceptions applies, and the same Ohio eviction materials explain the holdover exception in the possession context. Once the lease expired and Ms. Masten remained, K&D had the statutory path to possession that Indian Hills recognized; relabeling the dispute as a Fair Housing Act retaliation claim does not erase the holdover posture or the statutory limit on the defense.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the holdover exception applies, Count One was properly resolved on summary judgment regardless of the retaliation label.

attacks_proposed.argument: Section 3617 does not prove itself. The supplied Ohio retaliation materials say the defense must be established by evidence and discuss the dual-motive problem; they do not say timing alone is enough. Here, the brief relies primarily on sequence—protected activity, then nonrenewal, then eviction—and an OCRC probable-cause finding, but that does not, by itself, establish that the nonrenewal was because of protected activity rather than because the lease expired and Ms. Masten stayed beyond term.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without competent proof of causation, the FHA retaliation theory does not defeat summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Supremacy Clause argument overstates the conflict. The supplied authority on Ohio eviction law treats federal and Ohio fair-housing statutes as parallel sources of defense when discrimination is actually shown; it does not say the Fair Housing Act displaces ordinary state possession rules whenever a tenant invokes retaliation. Nothing in the authorities cited here shows that 42 U.S.C. § 3615 invalidates the Ohio holdover rule or Indian Hills' possession analysis.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If there is no actual conflict, the state court was not required to discard Ohio eviction precedent.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Chapter 4112 distinction is not enough. The brief assumes that because Chapter 4112 does not repeat the landlord-tenant holdover language, Indian Hills cannot apply. But the supplied Ohio materials still recognize the holdover framework in eviction law, and the fair-housing materials do not create a rule that a tenant who remains after lease expiration may always defeat possession simply by alleging retaliation. The absence of identical wording does not supply the missing right.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The Ohio Fair Housing Act theory still fails if the holdover framework remains applicable to possession actions.

attacks_proposed.argument: The public-policy attack cannot do the work the brief assigns it. The supplied materials show that retaliation defenses and holdover possession are governed by statute and established eviction doctrine; they do not provide authority for overriding Indian Hills on a generalized fairness theory. Put differently, policy concerns do not supply the missing statutory elements or erase the holdover exception the Ohio materials discuss.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If policy cannot override the statutory framework, the request to reverse Indian Hills on policy grounds fails.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is supported by the cited retaliation materials and it hits the weakest part of the federal FHA theory: causation. The brief does more than timing alone—it cites Matarese, the OCRC probable-cause finding, and the sequence of events—but it still does not produce direct evidence tying K&D's nonrenewal decision to protected activity. On this record, a court could conclude the retaliation theory is too inferential to defeat summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Ms. Masten aided another tenant, filed her own OCRC charge, K&D learned of that activity, then issued the nonrenewal; it also cites Matarese for the protected-activity/awareness/adverse-action/causal-connection framework and the OCRC probable-cause finding.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the record contains evidence of retaliatory motive beyond timing and the OCRC determination, and whether Ohio/FHA retaliation claims require but-for causation or only a motivating-factor showing.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited Ohio materials support the landlord's side more than the brief does: the holdover exception is a real feature of Ohio retaliation law, and source 24 expressly discusses it. The brief's answer is the statutory-text distinction between Chapter 4112 and Chapter 5321, but that step is underdeveloped. A court could accept the cross-application of Indian Hills and hold that the absence of identical wording in Chapter 4112 does not create a separate holdover escape from possession.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Chapter 4112 does not contain the holdover-specific language found in R.C. 5321.03(A)(4), so Indian Hills and Samsa should not control the Ohio Fair Housing Act claim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Ohio fair-housing precedent actually imports the Chapter 5321 holdover limitation into Chapter 4112 claims, and whether the cited Ohio fair-housing authorities recognize retaliation as a defense to possession after lease expiration.

judge_assessments.assessment: The Supremacy Clause point is legally real, but the attack is strong because the brief never cleanly identifies an actual conflict between Indian Hills/Ohio possession law and the federal Fair Housing Act. The cited authorities support preemption only when state law actually conflicts with federal law; they do not themselves show that Ohio's holdover rule is preempted. The brief does cite §3615 and preemption cases, so this is answerable, but if the court sees no direct conflict, the Supremacy Clause theory fails.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Ohio courts must apply federal law when state precedent conflicts, cites §3615, and relies on Michigan Canners, Swift, Wisconsin, and Larkin to say conflicting state law gives way.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Indian Hills or the Ohio holdover rule actually conflicts with a federal FHA retaliation defense, and whether §3615 invalidates only state laws that require discrimination or also state possession rules that incidentally limit defenses.

judge_assessments.assessment: The Ohio authorities do support the proposition that holdover status matters in the Chapter 5321 retaliation context, but that does not by itself defeat the federal FHA framing of this unit. The brief already answers by shifting away from Ohio landlord-tenant law and arguing that federal fair-housing rights survive the holdover label. So this attack has force only against the state-law strand, not the federal one.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Indian Hills should not bar a holdover tenant from asserting that nonrenewal and eviction violated the federal Fair Housing Act, and that federal law protects the tenant's claimed conduct and defense.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether §3617 or §3604(f) allows a retaliation challenge to a nonrenewal/eviction even after the tenant becomes a holdover, and whether the Ohio holdover exception can be imported into the federal FHA analysis.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is not a complete answer to the brief's last assignment. The cited materials and the brief's own argument show a policy concern, but they do not establish that an intermediate Ohio appellate court can overrule Indian Hills on policy alone. The brief already tries to ground the policy point in retaliation statutes and analogous public-policy cases, so the attack lands only as a warning that policy rhetoric is not a substitute for a doctrinal basis.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues Indian Hills is overinclusive, chills tenants from exercising rights, and should be reversed as against public policy, using Porter, L'Oranse, and Kinney as analogies.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the appellate court has authority to overrule Indian Hills and, if so, whether Ohio public-policy cases actually support doing so in a landlord-tenant retaliation setting.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack is unsupported on this record and misfires at a point the brief does not actually develop. It assumes a R.C. 1923.04 notice-sufficiency issue that is not the proposition under review and cites no authority in the supplied sources.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says K&D served an 81-day notice of nonrenewal and later a three-day notice to vacate, but it does not litigate the statutory content of the notice here.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is not a supported appellate attack on the propositions presented. It raises a service-method issue under R.C. 1923.04 without any cited authority and without tying the point to the challenged federal or fair-housing arguments.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the notice was served, but it does not discuss service mechanics as a live appellate issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This repeats the same unsupported notice-content theory. On this record, the court would not reach an R.C. 1923.04 form-of-notice issue because the brief's actual fight is over retaliation, holdover status, preemption, and Indian Hills.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief does not separately address notice wording beyond saying K&D issued nonrenewal and vacate notices.

results.verdict: partially persuasive but exposed on causation and authority
results.assessment: The brief has a usable structure and its federal-right framing is strongest where it insists that holdover status should not automatically erase fair-housing protection. But it is still vulnerable on the central causation point: it relies heavily on sequence, knowledge, and an administrative finding without directly tying the nonrenewal to protected activity. The cross-application of Indian Hills is also underdeveloped, and the Supremacy Clause theory needs a clearer conflict than the brief currently shows. The policy attack on the last issue is the weakest part because it does not supply a doctrinal basis for overriding or limiting Indian Hills.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. The cited authority does not support the brief’s broad statement that Civ.R. 13(A) is irrelevant to all prior eviction litigation. The source material cuts the other way: a possession-only FED is treated differently, but FED/back-rent proceedings can also include claims for rent and other damages. On this record, the brief’s answer is only partial because it does not clearly explain why the earlier back-rent/breach-of-lease case could not have been the forum for this injury claim. Appellees stand to preserve the res judicata ruling if the court treats the 2004 rent action as the operative preclusion case.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees overread Sherman and the authorities they cite. Those authorities at most show that Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply where the eviction complaint alleges only possession; they do not establish that every later personal-injury claim must have been asserted in an earlier landlord-tenant case. Appellees also rely on a 2004 back-rent and breach-of-lease action, but this record does not show that appellant’s separate tort claim was within the scope of that proceeding or that Civ.R. 13(A) required it to be tried there. Accordingly, appellees have not carried their burden to show that res judicata bars appellant’s claims as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the res judicata argument to what the authorities actually support: a possession-only FED does not trigger Civ.R. 13(A), and appellees have not shown that appellant’s tort claim was required to be litigated in the earlier rent case. Do not state a blanket rule that Civ.R. 13(A) never matters in landlord-tenant litigation.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even if the earlier possession case were excluded, the brief still has to show that the personal-injury claim was not logically related to the later back-rent case. It does not. Source 2 recognizes that rent-related tenant disputes are precisely the setting in which compulsory counterclaim principles operate, and source 8 confirms those cases can be joined with claims for other damages under the rental agreement. The brief’s common-area distinction does not actually answer the logical-relation question for the 2004 back-rent litigation it invokes.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a real logical-relation analysis, appellant has not defeated res judicata as to the later action.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real vulnerability, though not a knockout by itself. The brief does say the claim was not logically related to the back-rent case, but it mostly relies on the fact that the injury was not in a common area and on the Sherman/Haney distinction. That does not fully explain why a tenant’s personal-injury claim arising from the same landlord-tenant relationship would not be logically related to a rent action. The cited authority supports a logical-relation inquiry, so the court could reject the brief’s treatment as underdeveloped. If appellees win here, they keep the res judicata defense alive despite the brief’s attempt to separate the 2004 action.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if the Court considers the 2004 back-rent action, appellant’s personal-injury claim was not a compulsory counterclaim because it did not arise out of the same transaction or occurrence. The rent suit concerned alleged nonpayment and breach of lease; this case concerns a separate storage-room incident on September 26, 2002, in which appellant was injured when a six-foot table fell or was knocked onto him. The claims involve different facts, different proof, and different legal duties, and separate trials would not require substantial duplication of effort or resolve the same controversy. Under Rettig and Civ.R. 13(A), appellant’s injury claim was therefore not logically related to the rent action.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Add a direct logical-relation analysis comparing the back-rent case to the injury claim. The brief should explain that the two suits involved different operative facts, different evidence, and different legal duties, not just that the injury did not occur in a common area.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. Ohio respondeat superior requires a tort by an employee acting within the scope of employment, and the brief does not develop that link with much specificity. Saying employees controlled the storage room and were present there is not the same thing as proving the negligent act occurred within the scope of employment. The brief mostly speculates that the table was improperly stored or that an employee may have caused it to fall. That is thin support for vicarious liability, and appellees stand to avoid corporate liability under respondeat superior if the court treats the employee conduct as unproven or outside scope. The brief’s fallback direct-negligence theory may survive, but this specific theory is vulnerable.
challenges.suggested_response: The corporate appellees are not insulated from liability merely because the negligent conduct occurred in a room they controlled. The record shows that Ms. Ball, acting as community manager, arranged the cleanout, set the date and time, and directed appellant into the storage room, and that other management and maintenance personnel had access to and control over the room. From that evidence, a jury could find that the conduct giving rise to the injury occurred during the performance of the employees’ storage-room duties and within the course of their employment. At a minimum, the evidence is sufficient to submit the corporate-liability issue to the jury.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on respondeat superior as though control of the room alone proves scope of employment. Either tie the negligent act to an identified employee performing job duties, or soften the theory so it does not overstate what the record shows.

challenges.opponent_argument: The open-and-obvious defense is not wiped out simply because the object struck appellant unexpectedly. Source 24 states the general rule that a landowner owes no duty where a danger is open and obvious, and source 56 identifies only a negligence-per-se exception under R.C. 5321.04, which appellant does not plead here. The brief’s assertion that the doctrine 'does not apply' because a folding table hit him is not a legal rule and does not defeat the defense as a matter of law.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a weaker attack. The cited general rule for open-and-obvious danger is real, but the brief’s response is also substantial: appellant says he was struck by a table he was not knowingly confronting, so the doctrine’s usual rationale is not a clean fit. Source 56’s negligence-per-se discussion is not a direct answer to a common-law premises-negligence theory, so it does not do the work the attack claims. Still, the brief’s assertion that a folding table cannot be a dangerous condition as a matter of law is overstated, and appellees retain a plausible duty defense if the condition was plainly observable. The advocate loses mainly the chance to knock out duty on summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: The open-and-obvious doctrine does not entitle appellees to summary judgment on this record. Appellant was invited into the storage room for a specific purpose, and the folding table that caused his injuries struck him unexpectedly while he was in the room to retrieve his belongings. This is not a case in which appellant knowingly confronted a danger that was so obvious and apparent that he should reasonably have discovered and avoided it. At minimum, whether the condition was open and obvious, and whether appellees owed appellant a duty of ordinary care under these circumstances, are questions for the trier of fact.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tone down the open-and-obvious argument. The brief should not say the doctrine is categorically inapplicable because the table struck appellant; instead, it should argue that the record does not establish an obvious hazard as a matter of law and that appellant did not knowingly encounter the condition.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief states the Civ.R. 13(A) rules are irrelevant to the prior eviction litigation as a categorical matter, but the authority it relies on is narrower than that. Source 4 limits the Civil Rule 13(A) carve-out to an eviction complaint that alleges only possession, and source 8 shows a residential FED may also include trial on past-due rent and other damages under the rental agreement. The brief never explains why the later back-rent/breach-of-lease action could not have been the operative forum for this dispute, so its blanket res judicata theory is overstated.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the prior rent litigation was a proper counterclaim forum, the preclusion defense remains viable and summary judgment can be affirmed.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if the earlier possession case were excluded, the brief still has to show that the personal-injury claim was not logically related to the later back-rent case. It does not. Source 2 recognizes that rent-related tenant disputes are precisely the setting in which compulsory counterclaim principles operate, and source 8 confirms those cases can be joined with claims for other damages under the rental agreement. The brief’s common-area distinction does not actually answer the logical-relation question for the 2004 back-rent litigation it invokes.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a real logical-relation analysis, appellant has not defeated res judicata as to the later action.

attacks_proposed.argument: Res ipsa loquitur does not get appellant past the missing-proof problem. Source 39 specifically rejects the idea that control of a storage room is enough when the accident-producing instrumentality is a table and the exact cause of its movement is unknown; exclusive control must be shown as to the instrumentality that caused the injury. The brief proves only that appellees controlled the room, not that they controlled the table at the moment it moved, so the doctrine cannot fill the evidentiary gap.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If res ipsa fails, appellant must produce specific proof of breach, which the brief does not supply.

attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the doctrine remains available, appellees still have a complete duty defense to the common-law negligence claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The respondeat superior theory is unsupported because the brief never ties any employee’s act to the scope of employment with the required specificity. Source 69 makes scope of employment the controlling requirement and explains that keys or general control over a storage room do not themselves establish corporate liability. Here, the brief only speculates that the table was improperly stored or that a particular appellee may have caused it to fall; speculation is not proof that an employee committed a tort within the scope of employment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without scope-of-employment evidence, the corporate appellees cannot be held liable vicariously.

results.assessment: The brief has some traction on the open-and-obvious issue, but it is not yet persuasive where the case is most vulnerable. Its broad res judicata/Civ.R. 13(A) theory is overstated because the cited authority only clearly helps with possession-only eviction cases, while the 2004 back-rent/breach-of-lease action is not adequately addressed. It also underdevelops why the injury claim was not logically related to that later rent action. Finally, the respondeat superior theory is thin because it does not clearly tie any employee’s act to the scope of employment. The research does not settle those gaps in appellant’s favor, so those sections need the most repair.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands materially. The brief is right that a pure FED possession case is not the same thing as a later tort action, but appellees also rely on a 2004 back-rent/breach-of-lease case, and the brief itself acknowledges that a landlord's back-rent suit can trigger Civ.R. 13(A). Source 4 supports appellees on that point. The brief does answer with its alternative logical-relation argument, but that answer is not airtight on this record because it never squarely explains why the personal-injury claim would not have been a compulsory counterclaim in the back-rent action. If the court treats the back-rent case as the operative proceeding, appellant loses the res judicata argument.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees' res judicata argument fails on this record. Even assuming Civ.R. 13(A) can apply in a landlord's back-rent action, appellees have not shown that appellant's personal-injury claim arising from the storage-room accident was a compulsory counterclaim in the 2004 rent-and-lease case. The record before this Court does not include the pleadings or judgment from that action, and appellees therefore have not established that the accident claim and the rent dispute involved the same transaction, the same factual issues, or the same basic controversy. Appellant's claim concerns the separate issue of negligence in the storage room, not possession or rent due.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the res judicata section so it does not rest on a blanket FED exemption. The weakness for appellees is factual: the brief says appellant did not encounter a hazard he chose to confront; the table struck him, and the record suggests he noticed the table but not that it was obviously dangerous. challenges.suggested_response: Appellees' open-and-obvious argument fails because the doctrine applies to a danger that is open and obvious, not merely to the presence of an object in the room. The record shows only that appellant saw a folding table and was told not to touch it; it does not show that he knew, or reasonably should have known, that the table was unstable or posed an obvious risk of falling onto him. A six-foot table in a storage room is not, by itself, the kind of patent hazard that eliminates appellees' duty as a matter of law. At minimum, the question whether the condition was open and obvious was for the trier of fact.

challenges.suggested_response: Res ipsa loquitur applies because the circumstances permit a reasonable inference of negligence. A six-foot table falling or being knocked onto a tenant in that setting is the sort of घटना that ordinarily does not occur in the absence of negligence. results.verdict: Mixed: strongest on the fact-bound negligence theories, but
results.assessment: The brief is not yet fully persuasive as written. It has some real strength on the open-and-obvious and res ipsa points, where the record leaves room for a fact dispute and the appellees’ no-duty theories do not cleanly end the case. But two weaknesses need attention. First, the res judicata analysis is vulnerable because it leans too hard on a pure-FED framing and does not squarely defeat the 2004 back-rent/breach action as the operative compulsory-counterclaim proceeding. Second, the respondeat superior section is thin on scope of employment and leaves the employee-act issue too inferential. The record still does not settle the precise pleadings or judgment from the 2004 case.

The cited Ohio materials recognize an employee-tenant category, and the brief's own facts say Appellant was required to stay overnight and was given a room as part of the job. That means the record does not compel a non-tenant finding as a matter of law; appellees lose the clean summary-judgment posture on tenant status.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s testimony that she was required to stay overnight and was given a room as part of her caregiving duties does not establish tenant status. Ohio authority recognizes that an employee may be an ‘employee tenant’ when the employee leases and resides in residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment, but that is not what the record here shows. The undisputed facts are that no rental agreement was entered into, no rent was paid, and Appellant maintained a separate residence. On this record, the trial court correctly concluded that Appellant was not a tenant under Chapter 5321.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Acknowledge the employee-tenant source and distinguish it on the record. Make clear that overnight stays and a room provided as an accommodation do not, by themselves, establish a tenancy absent evidence of a rental agreement or lease pursuant to employment.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest where it insists the record does not show a clear tenancy and where it distinguishes commercial self-help cases from residential lockout rules. Its main weakness is that it repeatedly overstates the no-tenant point by leaning too hard on the lack of a written lease and separate rent, even though the challenges identify Ohio materials recognizing oral, implied, and employee-tenant arrangements. It also risks overgeneralizing the remedy issue by sounding broader than the record supports. The cited Ohio source says Chapter 1923/FED is not facially limited to tenants and landlords and that R.C. 1923.02 reaches occupants, including those without color of title. That undercuts the brief's move from 'Appellant was not a tenant' to 'FED was merely permissive or irrelevant.' The brief answers only by insisting there was no tenancy; it does not answer the separate point that non-tenancy does not take the dispute outside Chapter 1923. Appellee stands to lose the core statutory premise supporting the non-FED removal theory.
challenges.suggested_response: The argument is not that Chapter 1923 ceases to exist when a person is not a tenant. Rather, R.C. 5321.15(A) makes FED the exclusive remedy only in the residential landlord-tenant setting. Where the occupant is not a tenant under R.C. 5321.01(A), Appellant cannot convert the landlord-tenant exclusivity provision into a bar against other available remedies; the statute she relies on is not triggered.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the point. Do not say Chapter 1923 disappears or that FED becomes merely 'permissive'; say only that R.C. 5321.15(A)'s exclusive-remedy provision applies in the residential landlord-tenant setting, and Appellant cannot invoke that exclusivity absent a tenancy.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands only in part. Ohio materials recognize that a rental agreement may be oral and that employee-tenancy is a real category, so 'no written lease' and 'no direct rent check' are not automatically dispositive. But on this record the brief does have a strong answer: Appellant admitted no rent, no paycheck deduction, a separate residence, and no documents identifying Braemar as her address. The attack does not point to record evidence of an actual employment-based tenancy bargain, so it is answerable rather than fatal.
challenges.suggested_response: Ohio law does not make the absence of a written lease, standing alone, dispositive. A rental agreement may be written or oral, and Ohio law recognizes the separate concept of an employee tenant. But Appellant still must identify some actual rental agreement or other proof of tenancy; without that, the authorities she cites do not transform an employment-based occupancy into the residential tenancy required to invoke R.C. 5321.15(A).
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede the narrow point that the absence of a written lease or a direct rent check is not, by itself, dispositive. Recast the argument around the statutory definition of a rental agreement and the need for actual tenancy proof, and avoid implying that non-tenancy follows automatically from the absence of one form of paperwork.

challenges.opponent_argument: The cases the brief strings together are not a universal rule that every live-in occupant without rent is outside Chapter 5321. They stand for the narrower proposition that those particular occupants lacked a rental agreement and consideration; they do not resolve an employment-based housing arrangement, which Ohio’s employee-tenant materials treat separately. record_sources.quote: "The Landlord-Tenant Act... regulates the relationship between residential landlords and their tenants... An individual who lives in a residence with another without a rental agreement and without the payment of rent is not a tenant and cannot maintain an action for wrongful eviction."

challenges.judge_assessment: This is mostly a framing attack. The cited cases are fact-specific no-rent/no-lease decisions, and the brief already uses them for that narrower rule. The employee-housing wrinkle makes the analogy less neat, but the record facts are close enough that a court could still rely on the same no-tenancy principle. This does not by itself overturn the brief's core cases.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant's effort to recast these decisions as a universal rule is too broad, but the cases do supply the rule that matters: a rental agreement, written or oral, and the consideration that creates a tenancy. Ohio also recognizes that an employee may reside in premises pursuant to a contract of employment; that does not help Appellant unless she can point to an actual agreement establishing tenant status. The authorities cited by Appellant do not do that.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Acknowledge that the cited cases are fact-specific and that employee-based housing can sometimes create a tenancy. Then explain that the relevant common point remains the same: tenancy turns on an actual rental agreement and consideration, not merely on living in another's home.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief treats the absence of a written lease and a direct rent payment as dispositive, but Ohio materials are broader than that. A rental agreement may be written or oral, and Ohio’s employee-tenant materials recognize that a person may reside in premises pursuant to a contract of employment. On the authorities cited, the real question is whether the housing was part of the employment bargain and created a tenancy—not merely whether Appellant wrote a rent check.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court accepts this, the no-tenancy theory does not follow automatically from 'no written lease/no direct rent,' and summary judgment on the wrongful-eviction counts becomes vulnerable.

attacks_proposed.argument: The cases the brief strings together are not a universal rule that every live-in occupant without rent is outside Chapter 5321. They stand for the narrower proposition that those particular occupants lacked a rental agreement and consideration; they do not resolve an employment-based housing arrangement, which Ohio’s employee-tenant materials treat separately. The brief’s analogy is therefore overdrawn.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the factual analogy fails, the cited cases do not carry the broad affirmance the brief asks for.

attacks_proposed.argument: R.C. 1923.02 does not disappear just because Appellant was not a tenant. The statutory scheme is not limited to tenant/landlord labels; the Ohio eviction materials explain that Chapter 1923 is not facially restricted to tenants and landlords, and R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) reaches occupiers without color of title. The brief therefore overstates the consequence of non-tenancy when it says FED became merely 'permissive.'
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This undercuts the claim that Appellees could simply choose any non-FED removal method without implicating Ohio’s eviction framework.

attacks_proposed.argument: The sweeping statement that any fired live-in worker may be removed without an FED action if there is no separate lease and rent is not shown by the authorities cited. The brief turns a limited discussion of self-help in other settings into a general rule for residential premises, but Ohio materials recognize employee tenants and a contract-of-employment housing relationship. The court should not treat that policy gloss as settled law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If this argument fails, the brief loses its broadest justification for self-help removal of a former home-health worker.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief conflates 'FED not exclusive' with 'self-help lockout is lawful.' Even if Chapters 1923 and 5321 did not require FED exclusively on these facts, the brief still needs authority that non-FED removal of an occupant is affirmatively permitted. The cited Ohio materials do not supply that step, and the employee-tenant source cuts the other way by recognizing that employment-based housing can create tenancy rights.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: That missing step is fatal to the argument that Appellees' conduct was automatically lawful simply because Appellant was supposedly not a tenant.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands. The cited Ohio source says Chapter 1923/FED is not facially limited to tenants and landlords and that R.C. 1923.02 reaches occupants, including those without color of title. That undercuts the brief's move from 'Appellant was not a tenant' to 'FED was merely permissive or irrelevant.' The brief answers only by insisting there was no tenancy; it does not answer the separate point that non-tenancy does not take the dispute outside Chapter 1923. Appellee stands to lose the core statutory premise supporting the non-FED removal theory.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: If there is no tenancy and no rent, the brief says FED is permissive rather than mandatory, and Appellees could use some other removal method.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further Ohio appellate authority on whether R.C. 1923.02 independently covers non-tenant occupiers and what that means for removal methods.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a serious gap. Even if FED were not the exclusive remedy, the brief still needs authority that self-help removal of a former live-in worker is affirmatively lawful. The cited law does not supply that step, and the employee-tenant source cuts against a blanket self-help rule by recognizing that employment-based housing can create tenancy rights. The brief's statement that Appellees 'may elect to file FED' or remove without filing it is the weak link here.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says that because Appellant was not a tenant, Appellees were not limited to FED and could remove her without using FED.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research would need to confirm whether Ohio law actually permits self-help removal of a non-tenant occupant from residential premises, as opposed to merely allowing a non-exclusive FED remedy.

judge_assessments.assessment: This has force because the authorities cited do not establish a broad rule that any fired live-in worker may be summarily removed from residential premises. Ohio's employee-tenant materials recognize that housing can be part of the employment bargain. Still, the brief does try to answer with its no-lease/no-rent facts and by analogizing to nonresidential self-help cases, so this is not a clean knockout. The estate risks losing the broad policy justification for treating employment housing as outside landlord-tenant law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says that absent a separate rental agreement and rent, a former employee occupying the home as an accommodation to employment may be removed without FED, and FED is not the sole remedy.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Authority on whether Ohio recognizes a general self-help rule for former residential employees, beyond the commercial-premises cases the brief cites.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands only in part. Ohio materials recognize that a rental agreement may be oral and that employee-tenancy is a real category, so 'no written lease' and 'no direct rent check' are not automatically dispositive. But on this record the brief does have a strong answer: Appellant admitted no rent, no paycheck deduction, a separate residence, and no documents identifying Braemar as her address. The attack does not point to record evidence of an actual employment-based tenancy bargain, so it is answerable rather than fatal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says there was no rental agreement, no rent, and the room was just an accommodation for employment, with separate address records reinforcing that Appellant was not a tenant.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the record contains any evidence of an oral employment-based rental agreement, rent-in-kind, or other consideration creating tenant status.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is mostly a framing attack. The cited cases are fact-specific no-rent/no-lease decisions, and the brief already uses them for that narrower rule. The employee-housing wrinkle makes the analogy less neat, but the record facts are close enough that a court could still rely on the same no-tenancy principle. This does not by itself overturn the brief's core cases.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Ogle, Stone, and Amick support the rule that a person living with another without a rental agreement and without rent is not a tenant and cannot base wrongful-eviction claims on failure to use FED.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether any Ohio case squarely treats a live-in employee differently from the no-rent/no-lease occupants in Ogle, Stone, and Amick.

judge_assessments.assessment: Unsupported and not a viable appellate attack on this record. No cited authority is provided for the notice-form point, and the brief's dispositive theory is that FED was not required because Appellant was not a tenant. If the court accepts that theory, a R.C. 1923.04 notice defect is not reached. In any event, there is no record citation here showing the actual notice language.

This duplicates r6 and fails for the same reasons. The proposed attack relies on an unprovided legal rule and asks the court to reach a notice-form issue that the brief's tenancy/exclusivity theory makes unnecessary on this record. It would not move the appeal unless there were a record-supported FED claim and a cited defect in the notice itself, neither of which is shown here.

results.verdict: partially persuasive but vulnerable on the central statutory
results.assessment: The brief is strongest where it ties its facts to no lease, no rent, and no record proof of an actual tenancy bargain, and the no-tenancy cases give it some support. But it is exposed on the main statutory point: saying Appellant was not a tenant does not by itself answer whether Chapter 1923 still reaches the occupant, and the brief does not supply authority that removing a former live-in worker without FED is affirmatively lawful. The employee-housing wrinkle also leaves the exclusivity analysis underexplained. The broader framing attack on the cited cases is less damaging than the first two issues.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), the complainant must show the occupier is without color of title and that the complainant has the right of possession. The cited Ohio materials do support the general point that present title/right of possession matters in FED and that title disputes can defeat possession. On this record, the brief does answer with the probate orders, the February 1, 2023 deed back to the Estate, and its claim that Judge Grendell determined defendants lacked valid title. But the record excerpt does not fully remove the vulnerability that the defendants’ earlier deed and the later deed/order leave a title chain dispute, so this is not a trivial objection. If the court sees unresolved color-of-title or title-vesting issues, the Estate loses the FED predicate and summary judgment on possession.
challenges.suggested_response: Judge Grendell’s orders and the February 1, 2023 deed establish the Estate’s present title and right to possession. The Probate Court ordered the Cedar Road Premises transferred into the Estate, and defendants thereafter executed a deed conveying the Premises to the Estate. The materials before the Court further state that defendants occupy the Premises without color of title and that the Estate has title and the right to possession. On this record, no genuine issue of material fact remains as to the Estate’s right to present possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten paragraph 8 so it relies only on the probate order, the February 1, 2023 deed, and the record statement that defendants occupy without color of title. Do not imply the brief can itself resolve the earlier 2021 transfer unless the record contains an order or document expressly extinguishing that prior deed.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands only as a notice-compliance challenge, not as a complete knockdown. R.C. 1923.04(A) does require one of the statute’s permitted service methods, and the Ohio sources support strict compliance with the notice statute. But the brief expressly says the notice was served at the Premises, which is one of the statutory locations/methods for service, and it also says the notice contained the required warning language. The record excerpt is thin on how the notice was actually delivered, so the objection is answerable and could matter if Exhibit 12 does not show statutory service. It does not automatically defeat the motion on the face of this excerpt.

The notice also contained the statutory warning language in conspicuous bold print. Accordingly, plaintiff complied with the notice required before commencing this forcible entry and detainer action.
