attacks_proposed.argument: The motion assumes Civ.R. 56 governs this FED dispute in the same way it governs an ordinary civil case, but the authorities the brief itself invokes do not bridge that gap. The retrieved materials emphasize that forcible entry and detainer is a special summary statutory proceeding, and that ordinary Civil Rules can be inapplicable where they would undercut Chapter 1923’s structure. At most, the supplied record supports the general Civ.R. 56 standard; it does not establish the separate proposition that summary judgment procedure applies here without qualification.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Civ.R. 56 does not cleanly apply on the terms plaintiff assumes, the court should not grant partial summary judgment on a truncated record.

results.assessment: The brief reads reasonably well on the core FED theory because it asserts present title, the right to possession, and statutory notice, and the record has some support for those points. But the most serious weakness is the unresolved color-of-title problem: the motion does not clearly show that defendants’ earlier deed was voided, canceled, or extinguished, so the title chain still looks contested. The second weakness is notice: the excerpt says service was “at the Premises,” but does not clearly identify the exact statutory service method. The cumulative no-genuine-issue point depends on fixing those two defects; standing alone, it adds little. The research did not fully settle whether the record excerpt itself proves strict notice compliance.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest merits attack. Ohio authority the brief cites supports that present title/right to possession matters in FED, but the brief never clearly explains why a probate order authorizing the Estate to 'administer, manage, and sell' the property is enough, by itself, to create a superior present possessory right against occupants. The brief relies on Sed and its own conclusion, but the leap from management authority to eviction authority is still thin on this record.
challenges.suggested_response: The Probate Court ordered the Premises returned to the Estate, and defendants thereafter executed a deed conveying the Premises to the Estate on February 1, 2023. Because title was vested in the Estate and defendants no longer held color of title, the Estate had the present right to possession under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5). The April 11, 2023 order further confirms that the Probate Court vested the Estate with authority to administer, manage, and preserve the Premises pending sale; defendants’ continued occupancy is therefore inconsistent with the Estate’s superior present possessory right.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Reframe the point so it does not rely on the April 11 management order alone. The brief should rest on the Probate Court’s return order, the executed deed to the Estate, and the cited authority that present title controls possession, with the management order used only as additional confirmation of the Estate’s control over the Premises.

results.verdict: persuasive on the basic timeline, but exposed on the present
results.assessment: The brief has a workable core: it lays out the deed, the probate orders, and the notice timeline in a way that supports the Estate’s claim to possession. But its biggest weakness is still the same one the challenges flag: it does not convincingly show that an order to administer, manage, and sell the Premises is itself enough to establish a superior present possessory right and justify removal of occupants. It is also vulnerable on summary judgment proof, because the motion asserts admissible affidavits and exhibits without showing their foundation or competence in the excerpt. The notice argument is weaker than the merits attack, but it still leaves room to press strict compliance if the actual notice text is not made clear.

rule_audit.summary: A residential landlord owes statutory duties including compliance with building, housing, health, and safety codes and keeping the premises in a fit and habitable condition. challenges.opponent_argument: Baker never establishes the essential same-transaction showing for Civ.R. 13(A). The record shows Baker sued Friese for eviction, back rent, and property damage after the fall; it does not show that Friese’s bodily-injury claim was part of the same occurrence, or that it had to be pleaded as a compulsory counterclaim in that case. Ohio materials also distinguish between compulsory and permissive counterclaims in eviction litigation, which means Baker had to prove the injury claim actually fit Civ.R. 13(A), not merely that both disputes arose out of a tenancy.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a proven same-transaction match, res judicata does not attach and the prior municipal judgment does not bar this suit.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Baker's res judicata theory depends on showing Friese's injury claim was a compulsory counterclaim in the municipal case, and this record does not cleanly establish the same-transaction / logical-relation element. Baker shows only that the later case involved eviction, back rent, and property-damage claims after the fall; that does not automatically make a personal-injury claim arising from the stair condition compulsory. The cited landlord-tenant materials distinguish compulsory from permissive counterclaims, so this is a real gap rather than a phrasing issue. Baker's brief partly answers it by citing Adams, Haney, Maduka, Sherman, and by tying the injury to the tenancy, but it still does not supply a crisp same-occurrence analysis for these facts.
challenges.suggested_response: This was not a possession-only eviction. Baker's municipal-court action also sought back rent and property damages arising from the same tenancy at 15230 Thompson Road. Friese's claimed injury arose from the basement stairs in that same rental unit, and Friese himself alleged that the missing railing was the hazard at issue. On these facts, the claims are logically related and arise from the same rental relationship and premises condition. Under Civ.R. 13(A) and the landlord-tenant cases Baker cites, Friese was required to assert that claim in the municipal-court action or lose it.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strengthen the same-transaction paragraph with the actual facts in the record: same landlord-tenant relationship, same basement apartment, same stairway condition, and a municipal-court case that sought back rent and property damage, not just possession. That is the best available basis for the compulsory-counterclaim argument.

challenges.why_it_matters: If Chapter 1923 judgments do not automatically preclude later tort claims, Baker has not carried the burden of showing claim preclusion as a matter of law.

Because he did not do so, and because the municipal-court action proceeded to final judgment, this action is barred.

Q. ... was there enough light ... ? A. Yes ... Q. ... what happened. A. ... I missed the step."

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is only partly effective. It is true that simply knowing a staircase exists is not always the same as proving every feature of the stairway was open and obvious, and the landlord-tenant sources it cites say the open-and-obvious doctrine does not defeat R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claims. But that statutory point does not directly undercut Baker's common-law Armstrong argument in unit u9. Baker also has stronger factual support than the attack acknowledges: Friese used the stairs multiple times daily for nearly four years, said they were in the same condition as always, and admitted he had told Baker the stairs needed a railing. On this record, the open-and-obvious theory is not cleanly defeated.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese's own testimony shows that he used the basement stairs as his primary access three to four times a day for nearly four years, that the stairwell was adequately lit, and that he was always careful in using the steps. He also alleged that he had told Baker the staircase needed a railing. On this record, the absence of a handrail was not a hidden condition of which Friese was unaware. Baker therefore owed no duty to warn him about a condition he knew and repeatedly encountered. To the extent Friese attempts to recast the claim as one under R.C. 5321.04, he has not identified any applicable code or ordinance in this record.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the common-law premises-liability point, but rewrite it as a known-condition argument rather than a sweeping statement that the hazard was conclusively open and obvious for every possible theory. Do not rely on the doctrine to defeat a statutory landlord-duty claim unless the brief identifies an actual code provision.

It shows only that he knew the staircase existed, used it regularly, and was careful on it; that is not the same thing as knowing or appreciating a dangerous missing handrail. And Ohio landlord-tenant materials explain that the open-and-obvious doctrine does not apply to R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claims in the first place.

attacks_proposed.argument: Armstrong does not supply a blanket no-duty rule here. The retrieved landlord-tenant materials state that where a tenant invokes R.C. 5321.04, the open-and-obvious doctrine does not defeat the statutory claim the way it would an ordinary common-law invitee claim. Baker’s motion collapses those two doctrines into one and asks the Court to do the same.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: That framing would wrongly dispose of statutory premises-liability theories even if the stair condition was arguably obvious.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that a landlord has no statutory duty to install handrails is too broad. Ohio landlord-tenant materials say R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires compliance with applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes, and specifically note authority recognizing a duty to install a handrail on a basement stairway. Baker’s categorical no-duty argument therefore goes beyond what the cited Ohio materials support.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If a code-based handrail duty exists, Friese’s handrail theory cannot be dismissed as a matter of law on the ground that habitability never reaches stairs.

attacks_proposed.argument: The motion frames the issue too narrowly by treating 'habitability' as the only possible source of liability. Even if St. Germain and Taylor limit the general habitability doctrine, they do not answer whether a specific building- or safety-code requirement imposed a handrail obligation for this stairway. The complaint alleges a defective stair that needed a railing; that is a code-compliance question, not just a generalized habitability question.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the Court accepts Baker’s framing, it would ignore potentially independent statutory or code-based duties that could support liability.

attacks_proposed.argument: The res judicata theory overstates Ohio law. The retrieved landlord-tenant materials state that a judgment under Chapter 1923 is not a bar to a later action between the same parties on non-eviction claims. That cuts directly against treating Baker’s municipal-court eviction/damages case as an automatic bar to Friese’s separate personal-injury suit.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Chapter 1923 judgments do not automatically preclude later tort claims, Baker has not carried the burden of showing claim preclusion as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: Baker never establishes the essential same-transaction showing for Civ.R. 13(A). The record shows Baker sued Friese for eviction, back rent, and property damage after the fall; it does not show that Friese’s bodily-injury claim was part of the same occurrence, or that it had to be pleaded as a compulsory counterclaim in that case. Ohio materials also distinguish between compulsory and permissive counterclaims in eviction litigation, which means Baker had to prove the injury claim actually fit Civ.R. 13(A), not merely that both disputes arose out of a tenancy.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a proven same-transaction match, res judicata does not attach and the prior municipal judgment does not bar this suit.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack. Baker's res judicata theory depends on showing Friese's injury claim was a compulsory counterclaim in the municipal case, and this record does not cleanly establish the same-transaction / logical-relation element. Baker shows only that the later case involved eviction, back rent, and property-damage claims after the fall; that does not automatically make a personal-injury claim arising from the stair condition compulsory. The cited landlord-tenant materials distinguish compulsory from permissive counterclaims, so this is a real gap rather than a phrasing issue. Baker's brief partly answers it by citing Adams, Haney, Maduka, Sherman, and by tying the injury to the tenancy, but it still does not supply a crisp same-occurrence analysis for these facts.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The injury occurred first, then Baker sued Friese in municipal court for eviction and monetary damages arising from the tenancy; because Friese says his invitee status arose from the tenancy relationship, Baker argues the injury claim was a compulsory counterclaim under Civ.R. 13(A) and is now barred.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A court would need the actual municipal-court pleadings and a transaction-by-transaction comparison of the injury claim versus Baker's rent/property-damage claims.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has real force because source 56 states that a Chapter 1923 judgment is not itself a bar to later non-eviction claims. But Baker is not relying on Chapter 1923 alone; she relies on Civ.R. 13(A) compulsory-counterclaim preclusion and cites cases holding tenant injury claims can be barred when they should have been raised in the landlord's rent/eviction suit. So the source cuts against the motion in the abstract, but it does not by itself defeat the specific compulsory-counterclaim theory Baker advances. On this record, the court would reach the distinction, not simply accept the broad 'Chapter 1923 judgment' framing.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Baker says the prior municipal-court action went to final judgment on the merits, and under Love, Robinson, Civ.R. 13(A), and the landlord-tenant cases, Friese had to assert his injury claim there or lose it.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Resolution turns on whether the municipal case is treated as a Chapter 1923 eviction judgment only, or as a broader tenancy-damages action that can trigger compulsory counterclaim preclusion.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a legitimate overbreadth attack. Baker's motion says there is no statutory duty to install handrails, but source 22 says R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires compliance with applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes and specifically notes authority recognizing a duty to install a handrail on a basement stairway. That means Baker's categorical no-duty statement is too broad if an applicable code or ordinance exists. The brief does answer part of the point by relying on St. Germain and Taylor for the proposition that habitability alone does not make a missing handrail actionable, but it does not rule out a code-based duty. On this record, the attack matters only if Friese can identify a code violation.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Baker says Ohio courts have repeatedly held that a missing or defective handrail does not violate the landlord's statutory habitability duty, so Baker had no statutory handrail obligation.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The missing piece is whether any local or state building/housing code applied to this stairway and required a handrail.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is closely related to a3 and lands as a framing objection. Baker treats 'habitability' as the entire statutory inquiry, but source 22 shows the statute can also run through code-compliance duties. So the brief's framing is narrower than Ohio landlord-tenant law in the abstract. Still, on this record there is no identified code, ordinance, or expert proof that the stairway violated one, so the attack is not fatal by itself. It points out an omitted legal pathway, but Friese would still need evidence tying the railing to a specific code duty.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Baker says Friese relied on premises-liability law, not a landlord-specific statutory theory, and that the cited landlord cases say a missing handrail does not render premises uninhabitable.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Friese actually pleaded or supported a building-code theory is the determinative issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack is only partly effective. It is true that simply knowing a staircase exists is not always the same as proving every feature of the stairway was open and obvious, and the landlord-tenant sources it cites say the open-and-obvious doctrine does not defeat R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claims. But that statutory point does not directly undercut Baker's common-law Armstrong argument in unit u9. Baker also has stronger factual support than the attack acknowledges: Friese used the stairs multiple times daily for nearly four years, said they were in the same condition as always, and admitted he had told Baker the stairs needed a railing. On this record, the open-and-obvious theory is not cleanly defeated.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Baker says Friese knew the staircase, used it repeatedly for years, recognized the absence of a railing as a hazard, and therefore Baker owed no duty to warn under Armstrong.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A closer factual record on visibility of the handrail absence and lighting would matter, but the present testimony already cuts strongly against Friese.

judge_assessments.assessment: This does not really hit unit u9. Baker's open-and-obvious argument there is a common-law invitee-duty argument under Armstrong, not a R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claim. The landlord-tenant sources about the open-and-obvious doctrine not defeating statutory claims are therefore beside the point for this unit. Baker addresses the statutory issue separately in u12. So this is a category error, not a refutation of the cited common-law rule.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Unit u9 relies on Armstrong and the claim that the stair condition was open and obvious or actually known, eliminating the duty to warn under common-law premises liability.

judge_assessments.assessment: Unsupported on this record. No cited authority in the motion section you supplied says Baker had to plead or prove a 'reasonable opportunity to repair' as an element of her defense, and u1 is only a summary-judgment request plus a brief preview of the two defenses. This attack appears to import an element from a different statutory claim framework that Baker is not advancing here.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The motion seeks summary judgment based on open-and-obvious and res judicata theories, supported by Friese's deposition and the municipal-court record.

results.assessment: The brief has some real strength on the open-and-obvious and general habitability arguments, because the record does show Friese repeatedly used the stairs and the cited Ohio materials do not make a missing handrail actionable just from habitability alone. But it is still vulnerable where it matters most: Baker does not yet cleanly establish the Civ.R. 13(A) same-transaction requirement, and the res judicata theory overreaches if it reads the municipal-court case as an automatic bar. The other major weakness is the categorical no-duty framing, which is too broad unless the brief squarely addresses whether an applicable building or safety code imposed a handrail duty. The research did not settle that code question.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited landlord-tenant authorities do support compulsory counterclaims in some landlord/tenant disputes, and the brief relies on that line of cases. But the hard question is whether Friese’s separate personal-injury claim from a stair fall was the same transaction or occurrence as Baker’s later municipal-court rent/property-damage case. The brief tries to bridge that gap by saying Friese’s invitee status arose from the tenancy and by citing Sherman, Haney, Maduka, Lujan, and Adams, but the same-transaction requirement is still the vulnerable step. If the court draws a line between Baker’s rental/damage claims and Friese’s tort claim, the res judicata theory falls.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese’s injury claim did not arise in isolation; it arose from the condition of the leased basement apartment during the tenancy. Baker’s municipal-court action, in turn, sought back rent and damages arising out of that same tenancy and the same premises. Ohio authorities recognize that where the claims of landlord and tenant involve rights and duties arising from the rental agreement, the logical-relation test for Civ.R. 13(A) is satisfied. Because Friese’s claim and Baker’s prior action arose from the same rental relationship and the same leased premises, Friese was required to assert his claim as a compulsory counterclaim in the municipal-court case, and his present suit is barred.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: The brief needs to be more careful here: it should rely on the rental-relationship and logical-relation cases already cited, but it should not overstate that every tenant stair-fall claim is automatically a compulsory counterclaim. The best response is to say these claims arise from the same tenancy and the same premises, which is the supplied basis for Civ.R. 13(A), and then tie Baker’s prior suit and judgment to that same rental relationship.

The supplied record shows only that Friese used the stairs often and knew there was no handrail; it does not conclusively negate breach or causation, and any doubt must be resolved in Friese’s favor at summary judgment.

On this record, though, Baker does point to Friese’s deposition and the certified municipal-court pleadings/judgment, and the motion’s main theory is that duty is eliminated as a matter of law by open-and-obvious/known-hazard and res judicata. So the attack lands only if Friese can point to a concrete factual dispute that matters despite those defenses. Baker stands to lose the summary-judgment request only if the court finds the record too thin to decide the defenses as a matter of law.
challenges.suggested_response: Under Civ.R. 56, Baker has identified record evidence establishing the material facts relevant to her defenses, including Friese’s own deposition testimony and the certified municipal-court complaint and judgment. Friese’s testimony confirms his repeated use of the basement stairs, his awareness that there was no handrail, and the circumstances of his fall; the certified municipal-court materials confirm Baker’s earlier action for back rent and property damage and the resulting judgment. On this record, there is no genuine issue of material fact as to the facts material to Baker’s defenses, and Baker is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the Civ.R. 56 framing, but tighten it to the record evidence and to the legal defenses that can be decided as a matter of law. The response should say Baker carried her initial burden by citing Friese’s deposition and the certified municipal-court pleadings and judgment, and that Friese has not pointed to any material fact defeating the open-and-obvious/known-condition or res judicata defenses.

The record shows Friese was turning to close an outward-opening door, moving a bag, and stepping down when he fell. challenges.why_it_matters: If the danger’s obviousness is debatable, summary judgment on duty fails.

target.excerpt: Baker does not dispute that Friese was a business invitee. But an owner of a premises is not an insurer of the safety of invitees and is obligated only to warn invitees of defects of which they are unaware and unable to observe or discover for themselves. Armstrong v. Best Buy Co., Inc., 99 Ohio St.

record_sources.quote: "Q. And fair to say, you were well aware of the condition of the basement stairwell prior to your fall on January 16, 2021? A. Yes..."; "A. ... you have to be careful."; and "A. ... there was no handrail."

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a factual pushback on open-and-obvious. It has some force because Friese was turning, moving a bag, and stepping down when he fell, but on this record the alleged hazard is the stairway/absence of a handrail, which the brief says was well lit, frequently used, unchanged, and known to Friese. Ohio open-and-obvious doctrine usually turns on the condition itself, not the plaintiff’s movement at the moment of the fall, so this does not cleanly defeat Baker’s duty argument. Baker loses here only if the court treats the turning/misstep facts as creating a triable issue about whether the stair condition was truly open and obvious.
challenges.suggested_response: The relevant condition is the basement stairway and the admitted absence of a handrail. Friese testified that he used those stairs three to four times each day for nearly four years, that he was always careful using them, and that he knew there was no handrail. He further testified that he had to turn to close the outward-opening door before descending. Those facts confirm, rather than create, his knowledge of the condition. Under the open-and-obvious doctrine, a landowner owes no duty to warn of a danger that is known to the invitee or so open and obvious that the invitee may reasonably be expected to discover it.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue the fall mechanics themselves prove the danger was open and obvious. Instead, anchor the point in Friese’s admitted, repeated knowledge of the stairs and the missing handrail, and make clear that his act of turning to close the door does not create a duty where the condition itself was known and regularly encountered.

attacks_proposed.argument: Baker has not met the Civ.R. 56 burden to show the absence of any genuine issue of material fact. The supplied record shows only that Friese used the stairs often and knew there was no handrail; it does not conclusively negate breach or causation, and any doubt must be resolved in Friese’s favor at summary judgment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court sees unresolved factual questions, it cannot grant judgment as a matter of law on this record.

attacks_proposed.argument: Armstrong does not do the work Baker assigns it. Ohio landlord-tenant authority recognizes that premises-liability claims may turn on statutory duties, and a violation of R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) can constitute negligence per se that displaces the open-and-obvious doctrine. Baker’s motion never grapples with that body of law; it simply assumes that a handrail issue is governed only by common-law invitee principles.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If statutory landlord duties apply, Baker cannot win by citing Armstrong alone.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even on Baker’s own facts, the open-and-obvious theory remains a fact question, not a matter of law. The record shows Friese was turning to close an outward-opening door, moving a bag, and stepping down when he fell. That is exactly the kind of situation where visibility of the stairway does not necessarily eliminate the risk as a matter of law, especially when the record is viewed in Friese’s favor.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the danger’s obviousness is debatable, summary judgment on duty fails.

attacks_proposed.argument: Baker has not established the critical Civ.R. 13(A) premise that Friese’s personal-injury claim was the same transaction or occurrence as Baker’s municipal-court rent and damage suit. The retrieved authority discusses compulsory counterclaims in landlord-tenant cases, but it does not show that a tenant’s independent tort claim for a stair fall is automatically compulsory in response to a landlord’s later rent/damage action. At most, the materials show that counterclaim rules can apply in some eviction settings; they do not prove the bar Baker invokes here.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without the same-transaction showing, res judicata and compulsory-counterclaim bar fail.

attacks_proposed.argument: Baker’s res judicata theory is overstated because the prior municipal case, as shown in the record, produced a money judgment on Baker’s rent/property-damage claims—not an adjudication of Friese’s negligence/premises-liability claim. The fact that Baker previously sued Friese does not by itself make every later tenant claim compulsory, and the authorities cited in the record do not bridge that gap for this specific tort claim.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the prior judgment did not encompass this injury claim, it cannot preclude it now.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the ordinary Civ.R. 56 burden attack, and the cited summary-judgment source supports the general point that the movant must affirmatively show the absence of a genuine issue. On this record, though, Baker does point to Friese’s deposition and the certified municipal-court pleadings/judgment, and the motion’s main theory is that duty is eliminated as a matter of law by open-and-obvious/known-hazard and res judicata. So the attack lands only if Friese can point to a concrete factual dispute that matters despite those defenses. Baker stands to lose the summary-judgment request only if the court finds the record too thin to decide the defenses as a matter of law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The motion says there are no genuine issues of material fact, relies on Friese’s previously filed deposition plus certified copies of the prior municipal-court complaint and judgment, and frames the evidence as undisputed.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full deposition and any opposing summary-judgment evidence would settle whether a real factual dispute exists after the open-and-obvious and res judicata theories are applied.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attacks a statutory negligence-per-se theory that the motion does not actually advance. The brief frames the claim as common-law premises liability by an invitee and argues only open-and-obvious/known hazard; it does not invoke R.C. 5321.04 or any statutory-duty analysis. The cited secondary sources do recognize that statutory landlord duties can matter, but on this record that is not the motion Baker filed, so a court would not need to reach the objection as framed.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The motion relies on Armstrong and argues that the condition was open and obvious or actually known; it does not cite a landlord-duty statute or negligence-per-se theory.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Only a pleading or argument actually asserting an R.C. 5321.04-based theory would make this issue relevant.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a factual pushback on open-and-obvious. It has some force because Friese was turning, moving a bag, and stepping down when he fell, but on this record the alleged hazard is the stairway/absence of a handrail, which the brief says was well lit, frequently used, unchanged, and known to Friese. Ohio open-and-obvious doctrine usually turns on the condition itself, not the plaintiff’s movement at the moment of the fall, so this does not cleanly defeat Baker’s duty argument. Baker loses here only if the court treats the turning/misstep facts as creating a triable issue about whether the stair condition was truly open and obvious.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The motion emphasizes that Friese used the stairs three to four times daily for nearly four years, did not notice anything unusual before the fall, and even says he had told Baker the staircase needed a railing.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Photographs, layout, and any evidence of distraction, concealment, lighting problems, or a code-based stair defect would be the evidence that could move this from weak to real.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited landlord-tenant authorities do support compulsory counterclaims in some landlord/tenant disputes, and the brief relies on that line of cases. But the hard question is whether Friese’s separate personal-injury claim from a stair fall was the same transaction or occurrence as Baker’s later municipal-court rent/property-damage case. The brief tries to bridge that gap by saying Friese’s invitee status arose from the tenancy and by citing Sherman, Haney, Maduka, Lujan, and Adams, but the same-transaction requirement is still the vulnerable step. If the court draws a line between Baker’s rental/damage claims and Friese’s tort claim, the res judicata theory falls.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes Love and Robinson on res judicata, invokes Civ.R. 13(A), and cites landlord-tenant cases including Adams, Haney, Maduka, Lujan, and Sherman for the proposition that tenancy-based injury claims can be compulsory counterclaims.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The key point to research further is whether Ohio courts treat a tenant’s stair-fall injury claim as arising from the same transaction or occurrence as a landlord’s later rent/damage suit, especially in the specific procedural posture here.

judge_assessments.assessment: This misreads the doctrine. Res judicata of a compulsory counterclaim does not require the prior case to have adjudicated Friese’s injury claim on the merits; the theory is that the claim was barred because it should have been asserted in the earlier action. The brief already says exactly that. The better attack is whether the prior municipal case and this injury claim were the same transaction or occurrence, not whether the prior judgment ‘encompassed’ the injury claim.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says final judgment on Baker’s prior municipal-court action precludes claims that were or could have been litigated and that Friese’s injury claim should have been asserted as a compulsory counterclaim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: If the earlier case was not a compulsory-counterclaim setting, this objection would disappear; if it was, the prior judgment need not have decided the injury claim expressly.

results.verdict: Persuasive on the open-and-obvious defense, but still expose
results.assessment: The brief has real force where it uses Friese’s own deposition to show repeated use of the stairs, knowledge that there was no handrail, and the circumstances of the fall; that makes the open-and-obvious argument look strong. Its biggest weakness is the res judicata theory: the brief cites landlord-tenant counterclaim cases, but it still does not firmly establish that Friese’s personal-injury claim was the same transaction or occurrence as Baker’s earlier rent-and-damage suit. The summary-judgment showing is also only as strong as that legal framing, so if the court separates the tort claim from the municipal-court case, the motion is vulnerable.
